name: Rate Limiting
intent: Cap how many requests a client may make in a period, so no single caller (or bug, or attack) can use up capacity that everyone shares.
scenario: A public API serves thousands of customers. One customer's script has a bug and fires 5,000 requests per second, and the slowdown hits every other customer.
problem: Servers have finite capacity. Without a limit, one misbehaving or malicious client can exhaust CPU, connections or a paid downstream quota, and well-behaved clients suffer. Autoscaling is slow and costs money, so something has to say 'no' quickly and cheaply.

howItWorks.title: Identify who is calling
howItWorks.text: Pick a key to count against: API key, user id, IP address, or a combination. The choice decides what 'fair' means. An IP limit also punishes everyone behind one office network.

howItWorks.title: Token bucket: a bucket of permits that refills
howItWorks.text: Each client has a bucket holding up to N tokens. Every request takes one token; tokens are added back at a steady rate. An empty bucket means the request is rejected. The capacity N allows short bursts, and the refill rate sets the long-run average.

howItWorks.title: Reject early with a clear answer
howItWorks.text: A rejected request gets HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, ideally with a Retry-After header saying when to come back. Rejecting at the edge (gateway or load balancer) is much cheaper than letting the request reach the application.

howItWorks.title: Share the counters when there are many servers
howItWorks.text: With several servers behind a load balancer, each one counting separately would allow N times the limit. Counters are usually kept in a fast shared store such as Redis, updated atomically, or the limit is split across servers and accepted as approximate.

howItWorks.title: Pick the algorithm that fits
howItWorks.text: A fixed window counter is simple but lets a client send double the limit around a window boundary. A sliding window fixes that at the cost of more memory. A leaky bucket smooths traffic to a constant rate. A token bucket is the usual default because it permits controlled bursts.

pros: Protects shared capacity from one noisy or abusive client
Cheap to check, so it can run at the edge before expensive work
Makes costs and quotas predictable, and enables pricing tiers
Gives clients a clear signal to slow down
cons: Legitimate bursts can be rejected if limits are set too tight
Distributed counters add latency and a dependency that can itself fail
Choosing a fair key is hard (shared IPs, rotating IPs, many accounts)
Clients must handle 429s correctly, otherwise they just retry harder
whenToUse: Login, signup and password-reset endpoints, to slow brute-force attacks
Protecting calls that cost money or have a downstream quota
Multi-tenant systems where tenants share capacity
whenNotToUse: As the only defence against a real DDoS: that needs network-level protection
Internal calls where the right tool is backpressure from a saturated service
When you simply need more capacity and the load is legitimate
pitfalls: Counting per server instead of per client, so the real limit is N times higher
Failing closed when the counter store is down, which takes the whole API down with it
Not telling clients when to retry, so they retry immediately and make it worse
Limiting by IP only, which blocks whole offices and does nothing against rotating IPs
